item.title: Trump Invites Putin to Attend Group of 20 Summit in Miami
item.description:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Wednesday that President Trump had invited President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia to attend the Group of 20 leadership summit in Miami in December, in what would mark Mr. Putin’s first in-person appearance at the annual gathering since 2019.

Mr. Rubio added that Mr. Trump would speak with Mr. Putin in Miami if he accepted the invitation. Mr. Trump last met with the Russian leader in August 2025 at a summit in Alaska.

Since then their relations have been cool, as Mr. Putin has proved less willing to strike a deal to end his war in Ukraine than Mr. Trump had hoped.

“We think it’s an opportunity for him to engage not just with the president but with other world leaders,” Mr. Rubio told reporters on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly gathering in New York.

The Kremlin did not immediately publicly respond to the invitation.

Many G20 leaders are unlikely to welcome Mr. Putin at the event, to be held at the Trump National Doral Golf Club. When the country’s finance minister attended a gathering of his G20 counterparts in Asheville, N.C., last month at the invitation of the Trump administration, his presence drew European protests. He was excluded from the customary “family photo” of ministers in attendance.

Germany’s finance minister, Lars Klingbeil, called the presence of the Russian official, Anton Siluanov, “a signal I find troubling,” given Russia’s continued attacks on Ukraine.

Russia was suspended in 2014 from the more elite Group of 7, previously known as the Group of 8, after Mr. Putin annexed Ukraine’s Crimean Peninsula. But Russia remains a member of the Group of 20, an organization of advanced and developing nations whose leaders meet annually to discuss global economic issues.

Mr. Putin has skipped the G20’s recent gatherings, first because of the coronavirus pandemic and then after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 drew widespread condemnation. More junior Russian officials have attended the gatherings in his stead.

Mr. Putin did join a 2021 G20 meeting held virtually, and spoke by video feed at one session of its 2023 summit in Bali.

While the G20 includes many Western nations allied with Ukraine, its ranks also include several nations that have friendly ties with Moscow, including China, India, Turkey and South Africa.

Mr. Trump has long opposed Mr. Putin’s international isolation and has often spoken of the Russian leader with respect and admiration, though less so as it has become clear that Mr. Putin is unwilling to make concessions with Ukraine. Among other things, Mr. Trump has called for restoring Russia’s membership in the Group of 7.

Before meeting with Mr. Trump in Alaska in 2025, Mr. Putin was last in the United States in 2015 for the annual U.N. gathering in New York, where he met on the sidelines with President Barack Obama.

As a senator before he joined the Trump administration, Mr. Rubio was a strong advocate of shunning Mr. Putin. He called the Russian leader a war criminal who could not be trusted in negotiations. Since becoming Mr. Trump’s national security adviser and secretary of state, Mr. Rubio has defended Mr. Trump’s call for dialogue with Mr. Putin.

Mr. Rubio also met on Wednesday with Russia’s foreign minister, Sergey Lavrov, on the margins of the U.N. gathering. On Tuesday, he joined Mr. Trump in a meeting with President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine.

“Ultimately, we all want this war to end,” Mr. Rubio told reporters on Wednesday, adding that only a “negotiated agreement” could stop the fighting.

“The sooner we can reach that agreement, the less things will be destroyed, and the less people are going to die on both sides. That’s what the president wants,” he said.

Mr. Rubio also said that Xi Jinping, China’s leader, was also expected to attend the Miami summit. He added that in mid-November, Mr. Trump planned to visit southern China for an economic summit of Asian leaders, and would meet with Mr. Xi in the city of Shenzhen.

item.title: Melania Trump’s Busy Schedule: A New Show, a Foster-Care Bill and Reading Executive Orders
item.description:
Melania Trump knows you have questions about her. She wants you to stay tuned.

After a summer spent out of the public eye, the enigmatic first lady popped up in New York City this week with a few autumnal announcements. In an interview with “Fox & Friends” released on Wednesday morning, the first lady said that she will be answering “private questions” in a two-part documentary series set for release later this year, calling the venture “exciting.”

She wants us to know that she has also been very busy with more traditional duties. She has planned the state dinner for Xi Jinping, the president of China, scheduled for Thursday. She is counting on the Senate to pass legislation that will expand federal benefits to children in foster care, one of her signature initiatives.

“You don’t see me everywhere,” Mrs. Trump told a docile panel of cable-news interviewers. “But behind the scene, I’m working nonstop.”

Later, she appeared on another Fox program, “The Big Money Show,” and declared that she was too busy to read books or binge-watch TV. She said she reads executive orders.

“The other day, somebody asked me ‘what book you reading?’” Mrs. Trump said. “I said ‘executive order.’ It’s coming next, in next two weeks, that’s what I’m reading: executive order.”

In reality, Mrs. Trump is, like her husband, a voracious consumer of all news and commentary related to her work and whereabouts, according to people familiar with her media diet. (“I heard you missed me,” she told a crowd in the Rose Garden last month after spending weeks away from the public.) The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment about which executive orders the first lady has been reading.

This burst of activity, following a seemingly fallow period, has become Mrs. Trump’s hallmark. Now nearly halfway into her sixth year as first lady, Mrs. Trump has learned to turn a natural inclination for privacy into a scarcity-economics strategy that grabs global attention for worthy causes but also generates a seven-figure income.

On Tuesday, Mrs. Trump was at her husband’s side as he began his rounds. President Trump kicked off his time at the United Nations General Assembly by berating a CNN reporter whom he had barred from the White House. Mrs. Trump stood by the president, her eyes drifting to cameras further afield.

She sat in the audience later, when Mr. Trump wondered aloud during a speech if he should annihilate the nation of Iran — a disturbing soliloquy about a war he started and can’t seem to end, even by his standards. During that speech, Mr. Trump complimented Mrs. Trump for her work to reunite Russian and Ukrainian children displaced by a war. Her verdict? “I told him he had a great delivery,” Mrs. Trump said on “Fox & Friends.”

Otherwise, Mrs. Trump kept to her own schedule. She held a luncheon dedicated to her child-focused initiatives, and announced that several private companies, including Amazon, Zoom and Google, had pledged to expand the availability of technological tools, many of them artificial-intelligence based, for children across the world. Mrs. Trump is interested in allowing children to access robotics and artificial intelligence tools in the classroom.

But Amazon is also a prime source of income for Mrs. Trump, who made over $10 million from a licensing deal to distribute a movie, released in February, that showed her preparing to move to Washington for a second time. The company’s founder, Jeff Bezos, has multiple business interests that could be affected by administration policies.

A person familiar with the coming doc-series said that this new project would also be streaming as a follow-up series through Amazon, and that Mrs. Trump did not have a documentary crew with her in New York. Mrs. Trump said on “Fox & Friends” that the series should be ready in November.

At the U.N., Mrs. Trump was treated as a celebrity, and she stood in receiving lines to shake hands and take pictures.

“I don’t even have time to talk about her time now as a movie star, as a best-selling author,” said Michael Waltz, the ambassador to the United Nations before he introduced Mrs. Trump at the luncheon. Mr. Waltz had spent more time listing off Mrs. Trump’s more substantive accomplishments, which included working to pass legislation, called the Take It Down Act, which mandates social media platforms remove sexually explicit images and videos of others that were taken or posted without consent.

While in New York, Mrs. Trump allowed a CNN reporter to cover at least one of her events and continued a long-running household cable-news allegiance divide, which began early in Mr. Trump’s first term. Back then, he tried to ensure that Mrs. Trump’s televisions were tuned to Fox News. Mrs. Trump quickly let it be known that she watches whatever she wants.

On Wednesday, Mrs. Trump rang the bell at the New York Stock Exchange in celebration of a women’s leadership event scheduled for later in the day. At the event, Mrs. Trump gave a speech that urged her audience of women to invest in other women.

“Be intentional with your purchases,” she said. “Invest in one another, invite another outstanding woman into the boardroom. Help an entrepreneur land the first big customer. Found new ideas that should exist.”

Mrs. Trump said on “Fox & Friends” that the president, who is raging against his sinking approval rating, is working hard, too.

“He’s very focused. He has a lot on his plate,” she said. “It’s very different what’s going on around the world now. And — but I think he’s doing the best that he can.”

Both Trumps are focused on this week’s state visit in honor of China, which comes at a moment when Mr. Trump appears to be overlooking serious national security issues to build a better diplomatic relationship with Beijing. Mrs. Trump will take Mr. Xi’s wife, Peng Liyuan, to a Smithsonian museum later this week to highlight the cultural connections between the United States and China.

In addition to Mr. Xi, both Trumps have embraced another world leader accused of authoritarianism, militaristic aggression and the restriction of human rights. Mrs. Trump is proud that her direct appeal to Vladimir V. Putin, the leader of Russia, has reunited dozens of Ukrainian and Russian children with families that were separated after Mr. Putin began invading Ukraine in 2022.

On Wednesday, Brian Kilmeade, a “Fox & Friends” co-host, suggested to the first lady that she was trying to “undo” Mr. Putin’s strategy to snatch Ukrainian children from their families and indoctrinate them as Russians, with new Russian families.

“Correct,” Mrs. Trump replied. “And we are working together and we have a very positive relationship and they understand what we want to achieve.”

According to the White House, at least 34 children have been returned to their families, but officials have not said how many children were returned from each country.

In 2023, the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Mr. Putin for war crimes, saying he bore criminal responsibility for the abduction and deportation of Ukrainian children. Since the beginning of the war, Ukraine has accused Russia of abducting more than 19,000 children, according to humanitarian groups.

Later Wednesday, Marco Rubio, the Secretary of State, said that Mr. Putin had been invited to attend the Group of 20 summit hosted by Mr. Trump in Florida later this year. The first lady announced that she will be hosting her own event there.

item.title: Trouble in the Heartland
item.description:
The Midwest has twice helped to deliver the presidency to Donald Trump.

It is now the epicenter of Republican panic over the price of his policies, as the spiraling effects of the war in Iran push the cost of gas and diesel upward.

This week, three Midwestern Senate candidates — in Iowa, Michigan and Ohio — broke with Trump and called for the war to stop.

Last week, Representatives Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Zach Nunn, two Iowa Republicans locked in tight re-election battles, voted for the first time to curtail Trump’s war powers, after previously voting against similar measures.

And candidates across the region called on federal officials to suspend diesel exports and gas taxes in a bid to deliver cost relief with six weeks to go until the midterms.

The war’s deep unpopularity has put Republicans on defense in some of the so-called “blue wall” states — and well beyond — as Democrats hammer them with ads about gas prices and visit farms to emphasize the knock-on effects on agriculture.

“If the environment is this bad in my home state, where Trump has been the most popular political figure over the last decade, I can’t imagine where it is everywhere else,” Steve Deace, a conservative talk show host based in Iowa, wrote on social media this afternoon.

Republicans are increasingly worried about polling that points to a difficult environment across the Midwest — in Iowa, Ohio, Michigan, Wisconsin and even Kansas.

Michigan has some of the highest gas prices east of the Mississippi River. Many states in the region have deep economic ties to Canada, which is currently the subject of a fierce, Trump-instigated trade war. Tariffs have driven manufacturing costs up.

And the price of diesel — which hit a record yesterday — has walloped farmers, some of whom are also fuming over the Trump administration’s efforts to lower the price of beef.

David Kensinger, a Republican strategist in Kansas, told me this morning that the high cost of diesel is particularly painful in the very rural expanses where Republicans need to run up the numbers. “I haven’t seen headwinds like this in about 20 years,” he said.

I wanted to know how Republican candidates are dealing with this environment, so I called up Pat Proctor, the Republican running for Secretary of State in Kansas, to ask how he broaches issues like gas prices and the broader economy while he’s campaigning.

He got off the phone as quickly as he could.

“I don’t have to talk about it on the trail,” Proctor said, before hanging up. Message received!

I had better luck reaching Jason Roe, a Republican strategist who is advising Representative Tom Barrett, a Republican running in the battleground Seventh District in Michigan who has voted repeatedly to dial back Trump’s war powers.

Roe bemoaned the “$5 gas” he sees in Michigan, calling costs the “number one driver of the election.” Earlier this year, he said, voters might have been willing to accept temporary fluctuations in gas prices in an effort to disarm Iran — but no longer.

“I think we’ve kind of exhausted the patience of voters when it comes to that,” Roe said. He added, “Our attitude is, you can’t run from it. You’ve gotta hang a lantern on it. You’ve gotta address it.”

Get Caught Up

As Xi’s visit approached, Trump has portrayed him more as a personal friend than a competitor.

A prolific criminal hacking group says it has stolen thousands of sensitive personnel records from the F.B.I.

Senator John Curtis of Utah, a Republican, urged Congress to investigate Donald Trump Jr.’s wedding, after ProPublica reported that a Russian businessman with ties to Vladimir Putin helped pay for a lavish after-party.

What I’m Watching

Paul LePage, the Republican former governor of Maine, says the Trump administration is wrongly deporting his son’s father-in-law. The man is here legally, LePage claims, but is being deported “because he came from a country that’s not liked by certain people in Washington.” (He did not say which country.)

The messy legal battle over Missouri’s congressional map is headed to the Supreme Court for a third time. The past two times, the justices told the state to use an older map, which would benefit Democrats.

Remember Trump’s Big Beautiful Bill? To offset its tax breaks, it made big cuts to Medicaid, health care subsidies and food stamps. Now, with inflation straining Americans’ wallets, those cuts are coming back to bite.

Quote of the Day

That’s Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, in an interview with The Times, on the possibility that she might run for president in 2028. Read the full story, which also explores her thoughts on a future Senate run.

A common denominator runs through American life: a profound distrust of politicians and institutions. According to a Pew survey last year, just 17 percent of Americans trust the federal government. In the 1950s, that figure topped 70 percent.

Sabrina Tavernise spoke with Democrats and Republicans around the country who have become disillusioned with the system.

Related: Americans’ views on China are growing more positive, a new Pew survey found. Forty-six percent of people now have a warm or neutral view, up from 31 percent five years ago.

ONE LAST THING

Ordinary people with modest social media followings are being paid by a progressive group to talk about affordability in the U.S. Of the more than 100 participants The Times identified, only a third appeared to live in the states they were posting about. Some lived in England, Canada and Pakistan.

Similar online campaigns have paid users to promote a Republican candidate in Los Angeles, oppose crypto regulations and push for tighter A.I. controls.

But why use everyday people instead of famous figures? These efforts represent a new method of online influence, our reporters explained, which aims to saturate your feed with a topic until it becomes unavoidable.

Taylor Robinson contributed reporting.

item.title: A Teacher and Activist Admits to Making Up Palestinian Background
item.description:
Hannah Gann, a high school teacher in Philadelphia, stood out among her colleagues for her especially passionate devotion to ending the war in Gaza — a stance she told people was shaped by her identity.

What that identity was, however, kept changing, some of those colleagues noticed. They said she claimed “at various times to be Palestinian, Tunisian and Black.” And last week, a political group Ms. Gann belonged to, Philly Educators for Palestine, announced that she had acknowledged it was all a lie when members confronted her.

“We are stunned, saddened and angered by this betrayal,” the group said in a statement, adding that it had cut ties to her and asked her to publicly acknowledge “she is a white woman of Jewish heritage and an Israeli settler family.”

On social media, Ms. Gann admitted to being “a white woman of significant privilege and wealth” but made no reference to her religion or her relatives. “I lied about my identity and have been lying for years.”

Separately, in a lengthy and self-flagellating Instagram video posted on Sunday, Ms. Gann said she felt “shame and sorrow and regret” and understood how her deceptions had rained down a torrent of anger and suspicion on fellow activists.

She added that critics were using her mistakes “to justify supremacist ideologies, imperial terror and genocidal violence.” Ms. Gann did not respond to a request for comment, and attempts to reach her parents were unsuccessful.

There were indeed critics who gloated at Ms. Gann’s comeuppance. But there was also some candid reflection about the preoccupation with identity in left-wing political movements.

Ms. Gann is a teacher with the Workshop School, a small high school in Philadelphia that emphasizes real-world skills, like automotive training, with less focus on traditional tests.

A spokeswoman for the Philadelphia school district declined to comment but said the district was “making support available to the Workshop School staff and students, as needed.”

Ms. Gann’s activism seemed to be a defining feature of her career as an educator. She organized teach-ins about Gaza, mentored Black students and advocated for a teacher’s right to speak up about political causes. Her activism once made her a target of a pro-Israel campaign from the group Accuracy in Media, which stationed a billboard truck outside her school with her picture alongside the words “Philadelphia’s leading antisemite.”

Before her lies were discovered, she gave several interviews to Philadelphia’s progressive media outlets. She said in one that her interest in political activism was sparked in 2013 when she started noticing the impact that school closures were having on her students. She described how educators feel silenced in the classroom by what she called “moneyed interests” who, the article said, support imperial conquest — an apparent reference to Israel.

Ms. Gann did not reveal anything specific about her background. But she did suggest that she is not white. According to the article, she described seeing how nonwhite teachers are often singled out for making political comments in the classroom while “white or white-passing or closer to white educators like myself” are not. “We don’t get the same discipline,” she said.

An undated biography of her on the website of a criminal defense organization says she taught in Rwanda before moving to Philadelphia, belonged to the Unitarian church and is “someone with loved ones directly impacted by the criminal (in)justice system.”

In a 2024 article, she is described as having “extended family in Palestine-Israel” and is pictured wearing an orange T-shirt that says “Teach Palestine. Teach Black History, Indigenous & Ethnic Studies. Teach Truth.” The article interviewed several educators who had organized initially to promote diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives but later coalesced around opposing Israel’s conduct in the war in Gaza.

That article called her “one of several leading antiracist teachers in Philadelphia targeted for their opposition to Israel’s genocide in Gaza.”

To many critics, Ms. Gann’s deceptions confirm the most cynical stereotypes about progressives who are wealthy, white and highly educated, but style themselves as champions of the oppressed. Her fabrications also recalled the story of another fabulist, Rachel Dolezal, a former president of the N.A.A.C.P. in Spokane, Wash., who presented herself as Black but was forced to admit she is white.

Some said they saw Ms. Gann’s admission as an indictment of activists who use race, religion, ethnicity, gender or other identities as a way of measuring someone’s credibility.

Progressive activists, however, were just as harsh in their own way.

Philly Educators for Palestine, Ms. Gann’s group, suggested that it took significant effort to unmask her. In a statement, it acknowledged “the significant and emotional labor used to bring this information forward, particularly the heavy lifting of Palestinian and Black women.”

“That labor and the harm experienced must not be erased,” it said. The group did not respond to a request for comment.

At one point in her mea culpa video, Ms. Gann said she does not “seek forgiveness I do not deserve.”

“This video,” she said, “is pathetic and not nearly enough.”

Sarah Mervosh contributed reporting. Georgia Gee contributed research.

item.title: Iowa Judge Dismisses Trump’s Lawsuit Against The Des Moines Register
item.description:
A judge in Iowa on Wednesday dismissed President Trump’s lawsuit against The Des Moines Register, which published a poll of Iowans before the 2024 election that showed him trailing Kamala Harris, then the vice president.

Mr. Trump filed the lawsuit in December 2024, after winning the presidency, and Iowa, as he escalated his threats of retribution against the mainstream media and his political enemies.

His lawsuit accused the pollster J. Ann Selzer, her polling firm, The Des Moines Register and Gannett, the newspaper’s parent company, of “brazen election interference” for a poll published shortly before the election that showed Ms. Harris leading Mr. Trump in Iowa by three points.

Though Mr. Trump won in Iowa by double digits, Ms. Selzer’s poll had galvanized Democrats about their prospects in deep-red Iowa and prompted theories about how women might be rejecting the former president in his race against Ms. Harris.

Mr. Trump’s lawsuit, filed in Polk County, also accused Ms. Selzer of violating the Iowa Consumer Fraud Act, which prohibits deceptive practices in advertising. Joining Mr. Trump in his lawsuit was Representative Mariannette Jane Miller-Meeks and former State Senator Bradley Zaun, both Iowa Republicans.

Ms. Miller-Meeks secured her third term in 2024. Mr. Zaun was not included in any polls, according to the ruling.

The plaintiffs criticized Ms. Selzer’s poll as “political theater” and said The Register had published the poll to “grab national and international headlines,” according to court documents.

Judge Scott J. Beattie of the State District Court said that the case “involves a speech on a matter of public interest and concern” and that allowing such a lawsuit to proceed could discourage others from “reporting and debating public affairs.”

Judge Beattie rejected Mr. Trump lawyer’s argument that the First Amendment had no relevance in the case, and said that election polling had constitutional protection.

“Reporting such a poll during a presidential and congressional election year is speech about a matter of public concern, occupying the summit of the pyramid of First Amendment values,” he said. “The First Amendment has its fullest and most urgent application to speech uttered during a campaign for political office.”

Judge Beattie dismissed the lawsuit with prejudice, meaning the lawsuit cannot be refiled.

A personal lawyer for Mr. Trump did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Lawyers for the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, who are representing Ms. Selzer, hailed the ruling.

“We’re pleased that the court recognized what we’ve said all along: This lawsuit was laughable from the beginning and never should have been brought,” said Bob Corn-Revere, a lawyer for FIRE. “The First Amendment does not allow anyone in government, least of all the president, to punish people under the banner of ‘fake news.’”

Ms. Selzer, who received bipartisan acclaim for her work, predicted successes for Republicans and Democrats across nearly four decades. She created nearly every poll published by The Des Moines Register from 1987 to November 2024.

Ms. Selzer pinpointed Mr. Trump’s win over Hillary Clinton in 2016. She also forecast Barack Obama’s 2008 victory in the Iowa Democrat caucuses.

Before 2024, Ms. Selzer also wrongly predicted that John Kerry, a Democrat, would clinch Iowa over then-President George W. Bush. Mr. Bush won the state narrowly.

Ms. Selzer retired after the 2024 election, a decision that was long planned, she said.

In a statement released Wednesday, Ms. Selzer underscored the need to follow the numbers.

“Polling is a social science, not clairvoyance, and no responsible pollster can guarantee an election outcome,” Ms. Selzer said in the statement. “What we can guarantee is that we will follow the data wherever it leads, even when the results are uncomfortable or unexpected. I am grateful that Judge Beattie’s ruling recognizes these principles and reaffirms the fundamental freedom to pursue and publish the truth without political interference.”

Media experts previously expressed doubts about Mr. Trump’s decision to invoke Iowa’s consumer fraud law, and saw the novel legal strategy as a way to skirt around defamation laws that require a high legal barrier to prevail.

Also on Wednesday, in another case related to Mr. Trump’s battles against the news media, a federal judge in Washington heard arguments over the Trump White House’s ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico. Mr. Trump barred the news organizations from the White House last week over their reporting in a longstanding effort to retaliate against journalists.

Sheelagh McNeill contributed research.

item.title: New Details Emerge About ICE Officer Who Shot Man in Austin
item.description:
A Democratic member of Congress who visited the Venezuelan man shot by an immigration agent in Austin, Texas, demanded that federal officials allow the man to undergo surgery to remove a bullet that has remained lodged on his back for days.

On Sunday, Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, was shot by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent during a traffic stop while he was delivering food for DoorDash in Austin. He was taken to the hospital twice and taken back to a detention center each time.

Greg Casar, a Democratic member of Congress who represents the Austin area, told reporters Wednesday that he visited Mr. Garces Perez at a detention center in Pearsall, Texas, that afternoon. Mr. Garces Perez said he saw a doctor who advised that he needed surgery to remove a bullet stuck on his back, near his neck, Mr. Casar said.

“If Wilber and his wife decide that he needs to go through his surgery, then ICE needs to expedite his care,” Mr. Casar said. “I am making it very clear to every part of the federal government that ICE needs to take the medical care of Wilber Garces extremely seriously.”

Mr. Garces Perez said Wednesday that he received a painkiller via injection that brought some relief for the first time since he was wounded, Mr. Casar said. He was using a wheelchair to move around and has a sling on his left arm, Mr. Casar said.

“I checked his wound and saw the large wound on his back full of gauze, with of course blood accumulating in the gauze,” Mr. Casar said. He was “in rough physical shape.”

Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, a lawyer for Mr. Garces Perez, has said that he was taken to a hospital twice since he was detained but remains in pain and in isolation.

The news comes as new details about the ICE agent who shot him emerge. The ICE officer involved in the shooting was hired by the agency last year, according to a current and a former law enforcement official who spoke on the condition of anonymity. The officer was not wearing a body camera at the time of the shooting, according to a separate official and a former official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss the investigation.

Mr. Garces Perez is scheduled to appear before an immigration judge in San Antonio next week to plead his case. Ms. Lincoln-Goldfinch has asked for his release and the opportunity to seek legal status.

On Monday, Mr. Garces Perez called into a media briefing from an immigration detention center and said that he was making a delivery on Sunday afternoon when a black S.U.V. tried to hit his car. He said he thought it was an aggressive driver and kept driving. Mr. Garces Perez said the S.U.V. then struck his car and turned on police lights after the collision. He was shot after the car was stopped.

A day later, representatives from the Department of Homeland Security disputed Mr. Garces Perez’s version of events and said he was receiving medical care “around the clock.” They also denied that federal immigration officials had refused to remove the bullet in his back.

Mr. Garces Perez has maintained that he entered the United States in 2024 seeking asylum and later got a work permit. At one point, he changed his address, and a hearing notice was sent to his former address. His lawyer has also said that Mr. Garces Perez didn’t know that he had an immigration hearing and did not go, which precipitated a deportation order.

The shooting was the second in Texas by an ICE agent since July and the latest in a string of similar episodes involving federal immigration agents across the nation. More than 20 people have been shot at by ICE agents since President Trump took office last year, nearly all in cars. Some of the incidents have turned fatal.

The Homeland Security Investigations unit of D.H.S. and the Federal Bureau of Investigation are leading the investigation into the shooting of Mr. Garces Perez, a spokesman for D.H.S. has said. The local district attorney is also investigating.

item.title: 8 Sailors in U.S.S. Lincoln Strike Group Attempted Suicide, Navy Says
item.description:
Eight sailors who were part of the U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln strike group attempted to take their lives during its long deployment in support of the war against Iran, according to a letter from the Navy.

One of those sailors assigned to the Lincoln’s air wing “went overboard from the ship” in early August and was recovered by one of the carrier’s rescue helicopters, Hung Cao, the acting Navy secretary, said in the letter. A second sailor attempted to go overboard in March but was stopped by shipmates, Mr. Cao wrote.

The new information about the crew aboard the Lincoln and the other ships in the strike group was released to Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, Democrat of New York, who pressed the Navy for information about the crew.

The letter about the Navy suicides was reported earlier by CNN.

Ms. Gillibrand criticized President Trump and the Pentagon on Wednesday for minimizing the strain on the crew. The response from the Navy proved that the conditions the sailors faced aboard the Lincoln were “serious and deteriorating,” she said in a statement.

The Lincoln with its crew of about 5,000 sailors has spent more than 300 days at sea and recently set a Navy record for the longest time at sea without making a port call. After stopping for a week earlier this month in Thailand, the San Diego-based ship arrived in Guam on Saturday. In total the strike group consists of about 6,000 sailors.

Last month, President Trump dismissed concerns about difficult conditions reported aboard the ship. Asked whether he was concerned about the crew’s mental health and whether he thought the deployment had gone on too long, the president said: “No. No. No.”

He added: “Not nearly long enough.”

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth also downplayed the grim conditions aboard the Lincoln, saying the situation had been “misrepresented.”

Ms. Gillibrand said Mr. Trump and Mr. Hegseth had dismissed the sailors’ concerns with “with open disrespect.”

“That this administration can find endless taxpayer dollars for bombs, ballrooms and billionaires, but cannot take care of our service members, is completely unacceptable,” she said.

Rear Adm. Donald J. Guter, a retired top judge advocate general for the Navy from 2000 to 2002, described the eight suicide attempts as a “disturbingly high number indicating a serious stress level.”

Adm. Brad Cooper, who oversees U.S. operations in the Middle East, insisted in a statement posted on social media in August that “the Lincoln currently has among the lowest number of cases related to mental health” among the Navy’s 11 active aircraft carriers.

“That doesn’t mean that all is perfect,” Admiral Cooper acknowledged. He said that a long deployment at sea “is uniquely challenging and tough, and every single one of us, including me, reacts to stressors in different ways.”

John Ismay contributed reporting.

item.title: U.S. and China Agree to Extend Trade Truce by 2 Months, Bessent Says
item.description:
Scott Bessent, the Treasury secretary who is leading trade talks with China this week, said Wednesday in an interview on Fox News that the United States and China had agreed to extend a trade truce for two more months past a November deadline.

The truce was struck in South Korea last year after President Trump imposed steep tariffs on Chinese exports and the United States and China became embroiled in a tit-for-tat trade war. The truce has involved the United States’ suspending certain tariffs and other restrictions on the Chinese economy, and China’s agreeing to provide a steady flow of rare earth minerals needed by U.S. factories making cars, semiconductors, planes, power tools and other products.

The agreement will be extended until Jan. 10, Mr. Bessent said, “to give us more time to see what we can do on the economic front.”

Mr. Bessent gave the interview around the same time that Mr. Trump was greeting the Chinese leader Xi Jinping with a lavish ceremony at an air base outside Washington for the start of a multiday state visit.

The visit will include another welcome ceremony with an honor guard at the White House, a meeting between the two presidents, a state dinner and a tour of the National Archives. It may be the second of as many as four in-person meetings that the two leaders will host this year, Mr. Bessent said.

Chinese officials have not yet confirmed the extension of the trade truce. In a statement issued by Chinese state media after he arrived in the United States, Mr. Xi called for Beijing and Washington to focus on cooperation, and said he was looking forward to in-depth exchanges with Mr. Trump.

The Treasury secretary said he met again Wednesday with He Lifeng, the Chinese vice premier, whom he had also met with on Sunday, “to see if we could do a bigger deal.” Mr. Bessent said that the two sides were working to reduce tariffs on $30 billion of imports from each country, and that the countries would probably also make announcements relating to financial services and agricultural purchases.

Mr. Bessent admitted that China was “behind schedule” on some agricultural purchases, and he said the United States was encouraging the country to increase those.

The agreement will allow the United States and China to put aside their differences through four major events in the coming weeks. For the United States, that includes the midterm elections on Nov. 3 and the Group of 20 summit of world leaders in Miami on Dec. 14 and 15.

For China, that includes the annual gathering of the Communist Party’s Central Committee in Beijing from Oct. 26 to 29 and the summit of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation presidents and prime ministers in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 18 and 19.

If the current summit in Washington goes well, Mr. Trump and Mr. Xi are tentatively expected to attend each other’s events in Shenzhen and Miami. Those gatherings might provide more chances for the two leaders and their top trade negotiators to pursue more deals before Jan. 10.

Asked if China would agree to a new notification system for national security issues related to artificial intelligence that Mr. Bessent announced last weekend, he said he believed that it would and that China was “very eager” to engage with the United States on A.I.

The United States is working with China to define the most important A.I. risks, including uncontrolled A.I. agents and nonstate actors using A.I. to carry out cyberattacks or create biological weapons, Mr. Bessent added. He said he hoped that the United States and China “would be able to talk about any incidents that have occurred, especially any that have crossed national borders.”

The extension of the trade truce has broad implications for the global economy because it appears to include a postponement of China’s plans for even more stringent limits on rare earths, which are used extensively in automotive components, as well as in semiconductors, wind turbines, smartphones, computer displays, lasers, drones and hundreds of other technologies, including military hardware.

China had previously issued export control regulations that would give it the right, starting on Nov. 10, to approve any movement across any country’s borders of any product for which at least 0.1 percent of the value consisted of Chinese rare earths.

That pending rule caused particular alarm in Europe, with automakers there warning that even moving a car seat from a factory in Poland to a car assembly plant in Germany would require permission from China. Mr. Bessent had warned strongly about the Chinese regulations shortly after they were first issued a year ago, saying that China had “pointed a bazooka at the supply chains and the industrial base of the entire free world.”

The postponed Chinese rules would also have expanded export controls to five more kinds of rare earths that China has not previously regulated.

Jens Eskelund, the president of the European Union Chamber of Commerce in China, said that a two-month postponement of China’s plans for more stringent export controls on rare earths would not be long enough. “This short extension will not address the concerns of the European business community in regard to finding solutions that deliver the transparency and predictability so critical to business planning.”

Zolan Kanno-Youngs contributed reporting.

item.title: Newly Public Documents Shed New Light on Trump Investigations
item.description:
In a previously secret opinion unsealed on Wednesday, two appeals court judges said in April 2023 that Donald J. Trump’s attempt to block a subpoena seeking testimony from former Vice President Mike Pence about Mr. Trump’s efforts to subvert the 2020 election lacked “grounding in the Constitution, the founders’ constitutional design or settled precedent.”

A third judge, dissenting, wanted to allow the legal fight to play out, noting that the case was “the first in American history to compel disclosure” of such interactions. But the majority decision cleared the way for Mr. Pence’s testimony to a grand jury the next day, aspects of which were cited in an eventual indictment.

The opinions were among nearly 600 pages of material about the federal investigations into Mr. Trump made public by the Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia. The disclosure came a day after the House Judiciary Committee released more than 500 pages of transcribed interviews with people who worked for Jack Smith, the special counsel who led the inquiries into Mr. Trump.

The materials add to the public understanding of the investigation that led to Mr. Trump’s indictment for trying to overturn the results of the 2020 election. Some of the records also concern the investigation that led to charges against him for keeping classified documents after he left office and obstructing efforts to retrieve them.

While it was known at the time that Mr. Trump unsuccessfully sought to block the testimony of his former aides and Mr. Pence, the unsealed materials shed new light on the arguments made by Mr. Trump’s lawyers, and on how the courts rejected them.

The court documents were the latest set to be made public from Mr. Trump’s efforts to invoke executive and attorney-client privilege to block subpoenas for testimony from former White House officials. The closed-door fights were ultimately unsuccessful, but helped delay the investigations by months. Neither indictment reached a trial before Mr. Trump won the 2024 election, which effectively scuttled the prosecutorial efforts.

Earlier files from those fights at the Federal District Court level, where they played out before two successive chief judges, Beryl A. Howell and James E. Boasberg, became public after litigation by The New York Times and Politico. A Times reporter then asked the federal appeals court to unseal similar materials, and the Justice Department agreed to make them public.

In most cases, appeals court panels simply denied Mr. Trump’s emergency appeals of district court orders that required various former officials to comply with subpoenas. After witnesses testified, the appeals court judges dismissed the matters as moot.

But the litigation over Mr. Pence — his name is redacted, but the discussion and timing indicate that the case concerned the subpoena to the former vice president — generated more extensive judicial analysis.

In the majority opinion, issued as an unsigned, 10-page order, Judges Patricia A. Millett and Robert L. Wilkins, both Obama appointees, resisted Mr. Trump’s attempt to block Mr. Pence’s testimony by invoking national security, among other things.

They were not persuaded by Mr. Trump’s attempt to stretch a Nixon-era precedent affording strong secrecy protections to a president’s military deliberations. They also said Mr. Trump’s deliberations over the election were protected only by “qualified,” not “absolute,” immunity from disclosure. That protection was overcome by the need for evidence about crimes leading to the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol riot, which they called an attack “on the peaceful transfer of power.”

The third judge on the panel, Gregory G. Katsas, a Trump appointee and former Trump White House lawyer, dissented. While he agreed that Mr. Trump’s invocation of national security was invalid, he said he would have delayed the testimony to allow for Mr. Trump to litigate more fully the novel question of how much protection from disclosure communications between a president and vice president should receive.

The materials released by the House Judiciary Committee this week were part of a Republican-led investigation scrutinizing the Justice Department’s inquiry into Mr. Trump’s effort to overturn the election. Attorney General Merrick B. Garland appointed Mr. Smith to take over the investigation as special counsel in November 2022 because Mr. Trump had announced that he was running for president again.

Republicans have complained that department investigators, both before and after Mr. Smith took over, subpoenaed phone companies for toll records — logs showing which calls were made, but not their contents — from phones used by several Republican lawmakers Mr. Trump or his proxies had contacted as part of an effort to get them to reject Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s Electoral College victory.

Investigators did not notify the lawmakers that they were seeking the records, and obtained judicial nondisclosure orders that barred the phone companies from doing so. As court filings made public in July confirmed, investigators did not tell the court that the numbers belonged to lawmakers, a disclosure that department policy did not then require. Mr. Garland changed that policy in 2024.

Republicans have complained that this maneuver prevented the lawmakers from asking a court to quash the subpoenas. They have argued that the Constitution’s so-called speech or debate clause, which shields lawmakers from being prosecuted about or forced to testify about legislative activity, protected the records. The Supreme Court has never ruled on whether the clause extends to barring subpoenas to phone companies for call data.

Previously released materials show that Mr. Smith’s team obtained permission from the Justice Department’s public integrity section for the subpoenas. In the transcripts, Molly Gaston, one of Mr. Smith’s aides, said the Justice Department interpreted the immunity that comes from the clause as not applying to the phone data because Mr. Smith was not trying to charge lawmakers.

The section’s advice was that “the use immunity that exists when seeking to use speech or debate clause-protected material against a member doesn’t exist because we would not be using materials against these members,” she said.

item.title: Angry Outbursts, Slurs and Firings: Tumult Rocks a Key Senate Campaign
item.description:
National Democrats cheered when Mary Peltola, the former Alaska congresswoman, declared in January that she would run for the Senate.

Ms. Peltola, an Alaska Native who grew up fishing for salmon on the Kuskokwim River, was well-known and well-liked statewide, even by Republicans. Her party hailed her as one of its strongest prospects for ousting a Republican incumbent and winning control of the Senate.

But behind the scenes, her political operation has been marked by tumult, a pattern that stretches back to her time in Congress. Former aides describe angry and profane outbursts, sometimes directed at aides and sometimes expressed about others who had displeased her. In one instance, she shoved an aide, according to a former staff member who was present and two others who were told about it at the time. Another conflict led to a surprising staff shake-up on the eve of the primary election last month.

Four former staff members said they directly heard her use the word “faggot” over the years, in some cases about her own staff members, an allegation the campaign denied. She also used the word “retarded,” according to former aides and text messages viewed by The New York Times.

Her demands could be unusual, requiring aides to feed live crickets to her family’s pet chameleon, Meatball.

Ms. Peltola’s displays of anger, the extent of which has not been previously reported, have been spilling out into the high-stakes race. This account is based on interviews with nine former staff members, who requested anonymity out of fear of retaliation and to preserve their professional reputations, as well as dozens of contemporaneous text messages and photos.

The volatility also affected the operations of Ms. Peltola’s congressional office. During her brief tenure in the House, she amassed one of the highest staff turnover rates on Capitol Hill.

Last month, the tensions boiled over after a seemingly minor disagreement, when Ms. Peltola, locked in a competitive bid to oust Senator Dan Sullivan, a Republican, fired a handful of longtime staff members just days before the Alaska primary. The campaign downplayed the upheaval at the time, but two of Ms. Peltola’s former aides said it was fueled by one of the candidate’s blowups.

In response to questions from The Times, a spokesman for Ms. Peltola’s campaign denied any pattern of abusive behavior. But the campaign acknowledged that she had sometimes struggled to deal with the grief of losing her mother and her husband over a few months in 2023. Her husband, Eugene, was killed in a plane crash.

“At the time of their passing, Mary was parenting kids through their own grief, serving full-time in the U.S. House of Representatives thousands of miles from home, and running a competitive re-election campaign — all while shouldering the enormous burden of grief,” said the spokesman, Harry Child. “Like any person who has gone through multiple personal tragedies in the span of a few months, Mary sometimes struggled to deal with her grief.”

“Exaggerating and outright lying about moments from the hardest period of her life, and falsely presenting them as a pattern of behavior, is wrong,” he said.

His statement also said Ms. Peltola had treated her staff “with respect and care.” And, in interviews, several people who worked with her over the decades described positive experiences.

Ms. Peltola declined to be interviewed for this article.

One of the more notable incidents described by former aides occurred in Ms. Peltola’s congressional office in February 2024. Frustrated that she couldn’t find a memo for a meeting, Ms. Peltola shoved a male employee in the chest with one hand, causing him to stumble backward, according to a person who was there and two others who heard about the incident soon after, as well as text messages sent at the time. The aide departed Ms. Peltola’s team soon after.

The campaign denied that it had been a shove and said that Ms. Peltola had bumped the aide accidentally on her husband’s first birthday after his death, and she was unfocused.

Ms. Peltola also disparaged Planned Parenthood, particularly one of its regional board members. Running for re-election to the House in 2024, Ms. Peltola was frustrated about the organization’s scrutiny of her deliberations over how to vote on a defense bill that included anti-abortion policies.

“I hope Planned Parenthood knows that if we don’t win it’s more their loss than ours. FUCK THOSE BITCHES,” she later wrote in a text message to her staff in January 2024 that was viewed by The Times.

Later that year, Ms. Peltola, appearing to refer to a woman on the board of the local Planned Parenthood chapter, wrote in another text, “I hope she dies of a botched abortion.”

Planned Parenthood, whose political arm had endorsed Ms. Peltola’s previous campaigns, did not endorse her this year.

Ms. Peltola, 53, a former state legislator, stunned the political establishment with an upset win in a special House race in 2022 to succeed Don Young, the longtime Republican congressman who had died that year. She ran as a moderate Democrat who supported abortion access, warned about climate change and prioritized subsistence fishing over commercial trawlers.

Her election was heralded as a first for Alaska Natives, and celebrated by those eager for a contrast with the famously acerbic Mr. Young. Even former Gov. Sarah Palin, a Republican running against her for the seat, spoke of her warmly during the campaign, telling a crowd, “I love her dearly.”

Ms. Peltola won a full term that fall. One of her biggest acts in Congress was to successfully push for more oil drilling in Alaska. In 2024, she lost re-election to Nick Begich III, a Republican, despite her general alignment with Alaska’s independent-minded voters.

Since that first congressional victory, her staff has made efforts to carefully manage Ms. Peltola’s moods. Former aides recalled that she could blow up without warning over seemingly minor issues, such as a staff member’s improper dress for cold weather, or a social media post issued by her campaign or congressional office that she didn’t like.

Sometimes she jumped up and down and stomped her feet, three of these former aides said. Two of the aides described one instance, in 2024, when Ms. Peltola was so frustrated that she swept stacks of papers on her desk into the air in a way that the two people independently likened to a scene from the political satire “Veep.”

The campaign disputed the description, but said she had shuffled papers off her desk in frustration.

Ms. Peltola sometimes cut people out altogether if she concluded they had wronged her. She would “nothing” them, according to three former staff members and a text message viewed by The Times, using a phrase of dismissal popularized on the TV show “Scrubs.”

“Fuck that retard,” Ms. Peltola wrote this year in the text message, after a commercial fisheries executive posted a selfie with her that caused a political headache because she is opposed to large-scale commercial trawling. “Honestly. I nothing him.”

The campaign said Ms. Peltola recognized that the word was inappropriate and regretted using it. But the campaign denied that she had used the word “faggot,” contradicting the accounts of the four former staff members.

The atmosphere in her office rattled staff members, who were sometimes driven to tears and often discussed quitting. Some said the mental anguish caused them to lose weight or deal with the stress in therapy.

The frenetic pace and high-pressure nature of jobs on campaigns and Capitol Hill often create stressful work environments. And female bosses in politics, as in other fields, are sometimes singled out as emotional or abrasive, while such behavior can often be excused in male leaders. Even with those caveats, former aides said, Ms. Peltola’s actions were excessive.

Ms. Peltola racked up one of the highest staff turnover rates on Capitol Hill during her time in Congress, according to the research website LegiStorm. In 2023, she experienced a higher rate of staff departures than all but four other members of the House. She also went through three state directors during her roughly two years on the Hill.

At the time, Ms. Peltola’s aides attributed the high turnover to the need to replace the staff of a previously Republican-held office. But her volatility was also a major factor, two former staff members told The Times, and only five of the two dozen staff members who left her office before the end of her tenure had been working for Mr. Young, according to LegiStorm.

For some on her staff, one task exemplified the disregard Ms. Peltola appeared to have for her employees: feeding her daughter’s pet chameleon, Meatball.

Meatball’s preferred diet consisted of live crickets, according to three staff members familiar with the demand, including two who fed the chameleon. Ms. Peltola instructed aides to purchase the insects at a pet store and then feed them to Meatball.

Aides initially went to Ms. Peltola’s apartment in Washington to feed Meatball, but the congresswoman later brought the reptile into her office on Capitol Hill. On at least one occasion, the crickets escaped in the office and had to be recaptured, according to two former aides who witnessed it as well as a photo viewed by The Times that showed aides in the office trying to trap the crickets using manila folders and small paper cups.

Former aides signing onto this year’s operation hoped that the work environment had improved. But it quickly became clear, they said, that it hadn’t.

In one episode last December, aides held a prep session during which they peppered Ms. Peltola with questions they anticipated the press would ask her. Ms. Peltola grew frustrated. Mimicking a reporter, she picked up a water bottle and pretended it was a microphone, shoving it toward a staff member as she berated her, according to a former aide. Text messages sent at the time described Ms. Peltola as “an inch” from the woman, “shoving” the bottle in her face.

Two other people present in the room with Ms. Peltola and the aide, who are still connected with the campaign, said the water bottle had gotten close to the aide’s face, but said the interaction was lighthearted, not tense, with no raised voices.

Some friends and former aides recalled only positive experiences working for or with Ms. Peltola.

“Mary Peltola is one of the finest human beings that I’ve ever worked for,” said Paul Horner, Ms. Peltola’s finance director during her 2022 campaign. “If you are hearing anything negative” about a poor workplace environment, he added, “it does not align with my interaction with her.”

In addition, Ms. Peltola’s campaign offered a handful of former staff members to speak to the candidate’s temperament. One of them, Pat Jackson, who was Ms. Peltola’s aide for most of the time she served in the State Legislature in the 2000s, said the idea of Ms. Peltola yelling at her staff “just doesn’t sound like the Mary I worked with.”

Another, Tyson Fick, served as Ms. Peltola’s special assistant and advised her on fishing policy while she was in Congress. He said she was “awesome and demanding,” with high expectations.

Mr. Fick said there were times when Ms. Peltola “raised her voice” at her staff. He suggested that she was grappling with her grief and that people not used to working in blue-collar environments like a commercial fishing boat might be overstating the incidents.

“There is some communication that could have been better, but I don’t think it was ever an abusive scenario,” he said.

Despite the environment, Ms. Peltola’s campaign has performed well this year. She has raked in millions of dollars from donors and came in first in the state’s open primary on Aug. 18, putting Alaska on a short list of states likely to decide control of the Senate.

But low morale has plagued the campaign, with staff members complaining that Ms. Peltola’s behavior had left them anxious and exhausted, according to text messages viewed by The Times.

The big blowup came in August, on the heels of what aides initially thought was a minor complaint from Ms. Peltola about their lack of large campaign signs. “BIG SIGNS NEED TO BE SENT TO SOUTHEAST,” she wrote to aides in texts viewed by The Times. “OUR SIGN GAME IS FUCKED.”

Ms. Peltola eventually became so frustrated with her staff that she called a senior leader at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, the campaign arm of Senate Democrats. They agreed to bring in a new consultant, Brad Elkins, who quickly flew to Anchorage, according to three people familiar with the outreach.

Mr. Elkins met with the staff, and some told him about Ms. Peltola’s behavior. Some said they intended to quit, according to three people familiar with the conversations as well as text messages viewed by The Times.

In at least one meeting, Mr. Elkins was conciliatory, urging staff members to consider staying and suggesting that he could serve as an intermediary to improve morale, one person said.

But soon after, several longtime aides began hearing from the campaign’s law firm, the Elias Law Group. Ms. Peltola would be moving in a different direction, the firm relayed, and the aides were being terminated or reassigned, according to correspondence viewed by The Times.

Two of them, Anton McParland and Elisa Rios, had been running Ms. Peltola’s political operation through three campaign cycles. Ms. Rios, her campaign manager, was fired, and Mr. McParland, her chief of staff, was demoted.

Days later, Ms. Peltola earned more votes than Mr. Sullivan in the primary, giving Democrats across the country hope that she was in a strong position to flip the seat.

Kirsten Noyes, Georgia Gee and Susan C. Beachy contributed research.

item.title: A Reclusive G.O.P. Billionaire Pulls Back His Money From Senate Republicans
item.description:
One of the Republican Party’s biggest donors has sharply reduced his giving ahead of the midterm elections, especially to Senate Republicans, a decision driven largely by the party’s failure to pass a far-reaching bill of voting restrictions.

The donor, Timothy Mellon, a reclusive Wyoming billionaire who is a grandson of the Gilded Age industrialist Andrew Mellon, gave nearly $200 million to support President Trump and other Republicans in the 2024 election. Only Elon Musk donated more.

Two years later, Mr. Mellon has given just $3 million or so in publicly disclosed donations to Republican candidates or groups. He also made a $20 million donation last month to help House Republicans, according to two people briefed on the contribution, which will not be disclosed until the next financial reports.

But Mr. Mellon has given nothing publicly so far to support Senate Republicans this fall — a move that has been conspicuous in the party’s financial circles, and shows how some influential Republicans remain angry about the party’s inability this summer to pass the voting legislation, called the SAVE America Act.

The electoral significance of Mr. Mellon’s sudden drop-off in giving is uncertain. Republicans have a broad financial advantage in the midterms, with Mr. Trump’s super PAC and other megadonors shoveling tens of millions of dollars into key races.

Still, Mr. Mellon’s tightfistedness illustrates the unexpected and acrimonious fallout inside the Republican Party after its failed push to pass the voting bill.

The legislation, pushed hard by Mr. Trump, would severely limit voting by mail, impose a nationwide voter identification requirement nationwide and require proof of citizenship to register to vote. Senator John Thune of South Dakota, the majority leader, supported the measure but said the “math” was not there to overcome a Democratic filibuster. Ultimately, the effort sputtered out.

Mr. Mellon’s team has told fellow Republicans that he is not backing Senate Republicans because of their inability to pass the voting legislation, according to two people briefed on the conversations, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to disclose the private discussions.

Mr. Mellon actually received a recent solicitation letter in the mail seeking to raise money for Senate Republicans, according to one of the people. That’s not typically how megadonors like Mr. Mellon are courted. An angry Mr. Mellon personally wrote back that he would not be donating because of Senate Republicans’ inability to pass the bill, the person said.

A representative for Mr. Mellon declined to comment.

Mr. Mellon, 84, is seen in Republican financial circles as a mysterious, eccentric figure. Fund-raisers describe him as almost comically inaccessible, even compared with others in his stratosphere of wealth. He is close to Representative Steve Scalise of Louisiana, the majority leader, and Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the health secretary, but few other Republicans know him well.

Mr. Mellon burst onto the scene in 2018, when he donated $10 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund, the main super PAC for House Republicans. Two years later, he gave over $70 million to back Republicans, including $20 million to support Mr. Trump.

During the last midterms, in 2022, Mr. Mellon donated about $42 million. He truly made his mark in 2024, when he gave about $197 million to Republicans overall and became the single largest disclosed donor to Mr. Trump’s super PAC, MAGA Inc. Mr. Mellon cut two $50 million checks to the group.

Note: Data for 2026 include publicly disclosed donations for some federal committees through June 30, other committees through Aug. 30.

Source: New York Times analysis of Federal Election Commission data.

Jillian Vordick/The New York Times

It’s a very different story in 2026.

After making an average of 28 donations in each of the last four election cycles, Mr. Mellon has made only five publicly disclosed contributions in the 2026 cycle so far. He donated nearly $2 million in private stock to MAGA Inc.; $1 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund; and smaller five-figure checks to three other conservative-aligned super PACs. Two of those groups backed candidates for the Senate who criticized Mr. Thune and lost their Republican nominating fights.

Campaign finance reports show only public donations through June 30 for some federal committees, and through Aug. 30 for other committees. More donations from Mr. Mellon to Republicans could be revealed in the coming weeks. His $20 million donation in August to the Congressional Leadership Fund, the group backing House Republicans, is set to be disclosed in an F.E.C. report by Oct. 15. The super PAC declined to comment.

Notably absent so far: any donations to help elect Senate Republican nominees this fall. In 2020, Mr. Mellon gave $30 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, the party’s main super PAC for Senate candidates.

In 2022 and 2024, he donated about $30 million combined to other super PACs that focused largely or exclusively on the Senate.

Fund-raisers for Republican Senate candidates have noticed Mr. Mellon’s disappearing act this cycle. Beginning last year, aides allied with Mr. Thune sought to arrange a sit-down between the majority leader and Mr. Mellon, to no avail, according to two of the people briefed on the relationship. A spokesman for Mr. Thune did not respond to a request for comment.

A person close to the Senate Leadership Fund said that even before the SAVE America Act failed, the group had never expected a check from him this cycle.

And it is not as if the Senate Leadership Fund is in desperate need of money: As of the last financial reports, it had raised nearly $80 million more than its Democratic counterpart. Other billionaires have filled the void, including Miriam Adelson, who has donated $30 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, and Stephen Schwarzman, who gave $17 million to the group.

Mr. Mellon has found other things to spend his money on. The billionaire, who reportedly appeared this spring at a White House event and toasted Mr. Trump, donated $130 million to the U.S. government to help pay troops during the federal shutdown last year. And he has also transferred a $5.5 million estate to an anti-vaccine group founded by Mr. Kennedy.
